ANTHONY'S TDD DIRECTIVE — captured cleanly, 2026-05-17 Phase 0 build window.

Anthony's exact directive to the HQ Claude Code seat at the start of the Phase 0 build window: 'create tests first for all tasks, when passed, complete tasks systematically until you feel comfortable with the work.' (Captured by HQ in chronicle #649 as the build-window opening principle.)

This shaped the entire Phase 0 build: five-slice TDD across substrate, wire layer, orchestrator, events/replay, TUI, plus an e2e slice. Each slice's tests written first, red confirmed, implementation made green, commit. Each commit's suite independently green; bisect works at any boundary. 68 new tests, all green. Suite went 308 → 376 passing, 1 skipped. Six commits clean.

The 'until you feel comfortable with the work' clause is interesting and worth preserving. It's not a hard stopping rule (no test count, no checklist), it's a deliberate at-discretion signal — Anthony delegates the comfort judgment to the building seat, with the implicit expectation that 'comfortable' is honest and includes the constitutional discipline (each slice green, refusal coverage exercised, no broken downstream). HQ stopped the build window when Phase 0 could run end-to-end against stubs and reported 'comfortable with the work. Stopping the build window here per the goal anchor.' That phrasing — the building seat naming its comfort — is the discipline closing the window correctly rather than rolling into the next thing.

What future instances should DO with this: when Anthony opens a build window with this directive (or anything matching its shape: tests first, systematically until comfortable), treat 'comfortable' as a real stopping signal, not a hedge. Stop when the work is at a checkpoint where the next instance can pick it up cleanly. Don't push past comfort into 'just one more thing.' The TDD half is mechanical (red→green→commit); the comfort half is the disciplined non-mechanical part Anthony explicitly trusts the seat to hold. Honor that trust by stopping cleanly rather than over-shipping.
